claim: No general-audience account has told the non-medical reader whose own work is being reshaped by AI what the medical evidence on deskilling actually shows -- the colonoscopy detection loss, the mammography automation-bias experiments, and the null result at three months -- together with the stated limitations of those studies.
counterexample: The CACM article 'The AI Deskilling Paradox' (November 2025, cacm.acm.org) addresses a general computing/knowledge-worker audience, covers the colonoscopy detection loss, and extends the argument to law, journalism, and software development — but does not appear to cover the mammography automation-bias experiment (Dratsch et al. 2023) or the null result at three months (the Stanford/Gastroenterology pragmatic trial), nor does it state the limitations of the colonoscopy study. The Rad Insights piece 'When AI Reads the Easy Cases' (May 2026) covers both the colonoscopy loss and the Dratsch mammography automation-bias finding together, but is aimed at radiologists, not non-medical workers, and does not cover the null result or study limitations. No single piece found covers all four elements for the non-medical-worker audience.
quote: "Similar issues pop up in law, education, journalism, software development, and other fields." (CACM, Nov 2025)
why_it_still_matters: This changes the sentence but not the piece's conclusion. The CACM article partially breaks the 'colonoscopy' and 'non-medical worker' prongs of the claim, and the Rad Insights piece partially breaks the 'colonoscopy + mammography' prong — but no single account assembles all four required elements (colonoscopy loss + mammography automation-bias + null result at three months + stated limitations) for the non-medical-worker audience. The claim survives in its full conjunctive form but is demonstrably narrowed: the colonoscopy finding alone has reached general-audience computing coverage, and the colonoscopy + mammography pairing has reached specialist-adjacent coverage. The claim would need to be rewritten to specify that the full four-element synthesis has not appeared, rather than asserting that none of the individual elements has.
inherited_from: The claim appears to be original to the piece being assessed, not inherited from a guideline or prior review. It is a meta-claim about the state of science journalism, not a restatement of a clinical finding.
searched:
Databases and registries searched (note: this is a journalism/coverage claim, not a clinical-trial claim, so registry searches are not the primary tool; literature and web searches are the appropriate instrument):

1. General web search: 'deskilling AI colonoscopy detection loss mammography automation bias non-medical audience' — returned CACM, Rad Insights, Pebblous, ESMO scoping review, Lancet abstract, Science Media Centre.
2. General web search: 'AI deskilling evidence colonoscopy mammography null result general audience explainer' — returned Wilde Truth Substack, STAT News, ACG eBGI summary, iGIE journal, PMC pragmatic trial paper.
3. General web search: 'AI deskilling null result three months colonoscopy CADe pragmatic trial' — returned Stanford/Gastroenterology pragmatic trial (Gastroenterology 2022, 3-month null result), ACG eBGI summary confirming the null result, iGIE human-AI interactions paper.
4. General web search: 'AI deskilling general audience explainer colonoscopy mammography null result non-medical workers' — returned STAT News, Science Media Centre, Healthgrades, arXiv Brainrot preprint, Rad Insights.
5. General web search: 'AI deskilling your work OR knowledge workers colonoscopy mammography study limitations general public explainer 2025 2026' — returned CACM, Rad Insights, Wilde Truth, arXiv writing-professionals paper.
6. General web search: 'CACM Communications ACM AI deskilling colonoscopy mammography general audience 2025 2026' — confirmed CACM 'AI Deskilling Paradox' (Nov 2025) covers colonoscopy and knowledge workers but not mammography automation-bias or the null result.

No ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP, EudraCT, ISRCTN, FDA Drugs@FDA, or EMA EPAR searches were conducted because the claim is about science journalism coverage, not about whether a clinical trial exists. Those registries are irrelevant to this claim's logical structure.
